title: Σήματα καὶ ἀγορά
titleEn: The Signs and the Assembly — Odyssey 24.327–437
about: Laertes will not take the stranger on trust and asks for a sign. Odysseus answers with the scar from the boar on Parnassus, and then with the trees of the orchard that his father named for him when he was a small boy; at that Laertes' knees give way, and Odysseus has to hold him as he faints. Once he has his breath back Laertes calls on Zeus and the gods, but fears that the families of the dead suitors will rise against them, and Odysseus tells him to take heart and go to the house. There a Sicel handmaid bathes Laertes and Athena makes him taller and stouter, and Odysseus is amazed; the old man wishes aloud for the strength he had when he took Nericus. Dolius and his sons come in from the fields and are welcomed to the meal. Meanwhile Rumour carries news of the suitors' death through the town, and the dead are buried or shipped home. In the assembly Eupeithes, whose son Antinous was the first to die, calls for vengeance before Odysseus can get away to Pylos or Elis.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Λαέρτης ἀπαμείβετο φώνησέν τε·
sentences.l: Him then in turn answered Laertes, and spoke:
sentences.i: Then Laertes answered him in turn, and spoke:
sentences.n: Laertes, the father of Odysseus, now replies to the claim that closed the last part. τόν is the pronoun ‘him’, and αὖ ‘in turn’ is the short form of the αὖτε (αὖτ’ before a vowel) that stands in other reply-lines. ἀπαμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’. φώνησε is an unaugmented aorist (Attic ἐφώνησε) from φωνέω ‘raise the voice, speak’, with movable -ν before τε.

sentences.t:
εἰ μὲν δὴ Ὀδυσεύς γε ἐμὸς πάϊς ἐνθάδ’ ἱκάνεις,
σῆμά τί μοι νῦν εἰπὲ ἀριφραδές, ὄφρα πεποίθω.
sentences.l:
“If indeed Odysseus, my son, you have come here,
a sign to me now tell, very plain, so that I may trust.”
sentences.i: “If you really are Odysseus, my son, and have come here, then tell me now a very plain sign, so that I may be convinced.”
sentences.n: Laertes does not accept the tale he has just heard and asks for proof. εἰ μὲν δή γε ‘if indeed’ opens a condition whose answer is the imperative εἰπέ ‘tell’; Ὀδυσεύς is the predicate, ‘if you are Odysseus’. ἱκάνεις is a present with the force of a perfect, ‘you have come’, and ἐνθάδ’ is ἐνθάδε ‘here’. σῆμα is a ‘sign, token’ by which a person is known; ἀριφραδές ‘very plain’ has the intensive prefix ἀρι-. πεποίθω is the perfect subjunctive of πείθομαι ‘trust, be convinced’. πάϊς is παῖς ‘child, son’ with its two vowels kept apart.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: This reply-formula opens the paragraph, and the line comes again at 356 and 406 of this part with the same English each time. τόν is ‘him’, ἀπαμειβόμενος ‘answering’, προσέφη ‘addressed’ (the past tense of πρόσφημι ‘speak to’, with its augment). πολύμητις, ‘of many wiles’ (μῆτις is cunning intelligence), is Odysseus’s standing epithet and is translated every time, even though here he speaks to his own father.

sentences.t:
οὐλὴν μὲν πρῶτον τήνδε φράσαι ὀφθαλμοῖσι,
τὴν ἐν Παρνησῷ μ’ ἔλασεν σῦς λευκῷ ὀδόντι
οἰχόμενον·
sentences.i: “First, look with your eyes at this scar, which a boar dealt me on Parnassus with its white tusk as I went along;
sentences.n: The first proof is the scar, and the μέν here is answered by εἰ δ’ ἄγε in 336, where the second proof begins. φράσαι is read as the aorist imperative of φράζομαι ‘take note of, observe’ (the same spelling could be an active infinitive), with ὀφθαλμοῖσι ‘with your eyes’. οὐλήν ‘scar’ is picked up by τήν ‘which’. ἔλασεν is unaugmented (Attic ἤλασεν). Παρνησῷ is a dative of place for the mountain (Attic Παρνασσός); the boar’s tusk is called a ‘tooth’, ὀδόντι. οἰχόμενον, ‘going’, agrees with μ’.

sentences.t:
σὺ δέ με προΐεις καὶ πότνια μήτηρ
ἐς πατέρ’ Αὐτόλυκον μητρὸς φίλον, ὄφρ’ ἂν ἑλοίμην
δῶρα, τὰ δεῦρο μολών μοι ὑπέσχετο καὶ κατένευσεν.
sentences.l:
and you sent me forth, and my lady mother,
to father Autolycus, my mother’s dear one, so that I might take
the gifts which, coming here, he promised me and pledged with a nod.
sentences.i: You and my lady mother sent me to Autolycus, my mother’s dear father, so that I might receive the gifts that he had promised me, when he came here, and pledged with a nod.
sentences.n: Odysseus explains how he came to have the scar: he had been sent for gifts. προΐεις is the imperfect of προΐημι ‘send forth’, agreeing with σύ, though πότνια μήτηρ ‘lady mother’, added after the verb, shares it. In μητρὸς φίλον the adjective φίλον agrees with πατέρ’, so ‘my mother’s dear father’. ὄφρ’ ἂν ἑλοίμην is purpose with ἄν and the optative, ‘so that I might take’. μολών is the aorist participle of βλώσκω ‘come’; ὑπέσχετο means ‘promised’, and κατένευσεν ‘pledged with a nod’, since a nod of assent bound the giver.

sentences.t:
εἰ δ’ ἄγε τοι καὶ δένδρε’ ἐϋκτιμένην κατ’ ἀλωὴν
εἴπω, ἅ μοί ποτ’ ἔδωκας, ἐγὼ δ’ ᾔτεόν σε ἕκαστα
παιδνὸς ἐών, κατὰ κῆπον ἐπισπόμενος·
sentences.i: But come, let me also tell you the trees in the well-tilled plot, which you once gave me, when as a child I followed you through the garden asking for each one;
sentences.n: The second proof is the orchard. εἰ δ’ ἄγε is ‘come now’, and εἴπω a subjunctive, ‘let me tell’. δένδρε’ is δένδρεα with its final vowel elided. ἀλωή is a cultivated plot, not a building, and ἐϋκτιμένη is an adjective this part also gives to a town (377), so ‘well-built’ in the line-by-line layer is a stretched word for tilled ground. ᾔτεόν is the uncontracted imperfect of αἰτέω ‘ask for’ (Attic ᾔτουν), ‘I kept asking’. παιδνός is the poetic ‘small, a child’; ἐπισπόμενος is ‘following’.

sentences.t:
διὰ δ’ αὐτῶν
ἱκνεύμεσθα, σὺ δ’ ὠνόμασας καὶ ἔειπες ἕκαστα.
sentences.l:
and through them
we went, and you named and told me each.
sentences.i: We went through them, and you named each one and told me of it.
sentences.n: ἱκνεύμεσθα is the first plural imperfect of ἱκνέομαι ‘come to, pass through’, with the ending -μεσθα where Attic has -μεθα; ‘we kept going through them’. αὐτῶν means the trees. ὠνόμασας is the aorist of ὀνομάζω ‘name’, and ἔειπες the aorist of the verb ‘say’ with the old doubled vowel (Attic εἶπες). ἕκαστα, ‘each thing’, repeats the word of 337: the boy asked for each tree, and his father named each one.

sentences.t:
ὄγχνας μοι δῶκας τρισκαίδεκα καὶ δέκα μηλέας,
συκέας τεσσαράκοντ’·
sentences.l:
Pear trees to me you gave, thirteen, and ten apple trees,
fig trees forty;
sentences.i: You gave me thirteen pear trees and ten apple trees, and forty fig trees;
sentences.n: The count of the trees begins. ὄγχνας ‘pear trees’, μηλέας ‘apple trees’ and συκέας ‘fig trees’ are accusatives in -ας, συκέας uncontracted. δῶκας is an aorist without augment (Attic ἔδωκας). τρισκαίδεκα is ‘thirteen’, and τεσσαράκοντ’ is τεσσαράκοντα with its last vowel elided.

sentences.t:
ὄρχους δέ μοι ὧδ’ ὀνόμηνας
δώσειν πεντήκοντα, διατρύγιος δὲ ἕκαστος
ἤην·
sentences.i: And so you named for me fifty rows of vines that you would give me, each one yielding a vintage;
sentences.n: ὄρχους, accusative of ὄρχος, is a ‘row’ of vines or trees. ὧδ’ ὀνόμηνας δώσειν is ‘you named thus that you would give’, with the future infinitive in indirect speech. διατρύγιος is a rare word whose meaning is uncertain: it is built on διά and τρύγη ‘vintage’, and the usual guesses are ‘ripening at different times through the season’ and ‘yielding a vintage of its own’; the translation says only ‘yielding a vintage’. ἤην is the epic form of ἦν.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δ’ ἀνὰ σταφυλαὶ παντοῖαι ἔασιν—
ὁππότε δὴ Διὸς ὧραι ἐπιβρίσειαν ὕπερθεν.
sentences.l:
and there upon them clusters of every kind are —
whenever the seasons of Zeus have pressed down from above.”
sentences.i: and on them are grapes of every kind, whenever the seasons of Zeus have weighed down on them from above.”
sentences.n: This unit closes Odysseus’s speech, and Murray’s dash marks the break before the clause of time. ἀνά is an adverb here, ‘upon them’, and ἔασιν is the epic third plural of εἰμί (Attic εἰσίν). ὁππότε with the optative ἐπιβρίσειαν means ‘whenever’ of something that happens again and again; ἐπιβρίθω is ‘press upon, be heavy upon’. Διὸς ὧραι ‘the seasons of Zeus’ are the seasons of the year, presumably those that ripen the grapes, though the Greek does not say so; ὕπερθεν has the suffix -θεν ‘from’.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τοῦ δ’ αὐτοῦ λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ,
σήματ’ ἀναγνόντος τά οἱ ἔμπεδα πέφραδ’ Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and then his knees were loosed, and his dear heart,
in him who recognised the signs which Odysseus had told him, sure ones.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and his knees gave way at once, and his heart too, as he recognised the sure signs which Odysseus had told him.
sentences.n: The signs have convinced Laertes, and he is overcome. This paragraph begins with the formula for being overcome. τοῦ is the pronoun ‘his’, and αὐτοῦ is the adverb ‘on the spot’. λύτο is an aorist of λύω ‘loosen’ without augment. ἀναγνόντος, a genitive participle agreeing with τοῦ, is from ἀναγιγνώσκω ‘know again, recognise’. ἔμπεδα, ‘firm, sure’, goes with σήματα, and πέφραδ’ is πέφραδε, the reduplicated aorist of φράζω ‘point out, tell’.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δὲ παιδὶ φίλῳ βάλε πήχεε·
sentences.l: And around his dear child he threw his arms;
sentences.i: He threw his arms around his dear son;
sentences.n: The subject is Laertes, the τοῦ of 345, and the ‘dear child’ is Odysseus, who is named again at the end of the sentence that follows. ἀμφί … βάλε is tmesis, ‘threw around’, and βάλε is unaugmented (Attic ἔβαλε). πήχεε is a dual, ‘his two arms’; παιδί and φίλῳ are datives.

sentences.t:
τὸν δὲ ποτὶ οἷ
εἷλεν ἀποψύχοντα πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς.
sentences.l:
and him toward himself
took, fainting, much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus.
sentences.i: and much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus took him to himself as he fainted.
sentences.n: The subject changes: τόν is Laertes, and Odysseus, the subject, is held back to the end of the sentence. ποτὶ οἷ is ‘close to himself’, οἷ being the dative of the pronoun ἕ after ποτί. εἷλεν is the aorist of αἱρέω, ‘took, caught’. ἀποψύχοντα, from ἀποψύχω ‘breathe out’, is here a faint, not a death, since Laertes comes to himself in the next line. The two epithets of Odysseus are given in full, as always: πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’ and δῖος ‘heavenly’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἄμπνυτο καὶ ἐς φρένα θυμὸς ἀγέρθη,
ἐξαῦτις μύθοισιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπε·
sentences.l:
But when then he revived, and into his wits his spirit was gathered back,
once more with words, answering, he addressed (them):
sentences.i: But when he had revived, and his spirit had gathered itself back into his wits, he answered and spoke again in these words:
sentences.n: The subject is again Laertes. ἄμπνυτο is the aorist middle of ἀναπνέω ‘get one’s breath back, revive’, without augment and with the preverb shortened to ἀν- and then ἀμ- before π; ἀγέρθη is the aorist passive of ἀγείρω ‘gather’. ῥ’ is ῥα. ἐξαῦτις is ‘once more’. προσέειπε has no expressed object; the ‘(them)’ of the line-by-line layer is the gods, since what follows is addressed to Zeus and to all the gods.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ, ἦ ῥα ἔτ’ ἔστε θεοὶ κατὰ μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον,
εἰ ἐτεὸν μνηστῆρες ἀτάσθαλον ὕβριν ἔτισαν.
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, truly then still you are, gods, on long Olympus,
if in truth the suitors wanton insolence have paid for.
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, so you gods are still there on tall Olympus, if the suitors have truly paid for their wanton insolence.
sentences.n: Laertes turns to the gods, half in wonder and half in doubt. Ζεῦ πάτερ is ‘Father Zeus’. ἦ ῥα means ‘so it is true that’, and ἔστε is the second plural ‘you are’, said to all the gods; κατά with the accusative gives ‘along, on’. ἐτεόν is an adverb, ‘truly’. ἔτισαν is the aorist of τίνω ‘pay, pay for’, so the suitors ‘paid for’ their ὕβρις ‘insolence’; ἀτάσθαλον ‘wanton’ is the adjective of the ἀτασθαλίαι ‘wanton follies’ of 1.7.

sentences.t:
νῦν δ’ αἰνῶς δείδοικα κατὰ φρένα μὴ τάχα πάντες
ἐνθάδ’ ἐπέλθωσιν Ἰθακήσιοι, ἀγγελίας δὲ
πάντη ἐποτρύνωσι Κεφαλλήνων πολίεσσι.
sentences.l:
But now terribly I fear in my mind lest soon all
the Ithacans come upon us here, and news
everywhere speed on to the cities of the Cephallenians.”
sentences.i: But now I am terribly afraid in my mind that all the Ithacans may soon come down on us here and speed the news everywhere to the cities of the Cephallenians.”
sentences.n: Laertes’ fear is about the dead suitors’ families and the people of Ithaca. νῦν δέ is ‘but as things are’. αἰνῶς ‘terribly’ comes from αἰνός ‘fearsome’, and δείδοικα is the perfect of δείδω ‘fear’. μὴ … ἐπέλθωσιν is a fear-clause with the subjunctive, ‘lest they come upon (us)’, the object being understood. Ἰθακήσιοι are the men of Ithaca, and the Κεφαλλῆνες are the wider people to whom they belong. ἀγγελίας is accusative plural, ‘news’, the object of ἐποτρύνωσι ‘speed on, urge on’, with πολίεσσι ‘to the cities’ in the dative.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: This is the same reply-formula as 330 and 406, translated the same way each time. Here Odysseus answers his father’s fear, and the speech that follows at 357 is his.

sentences.t: θάρσει, μή τοι ταῦτα μετὰ φρεσὶ σῇσι μελόντων.
sentences.l: “Take courage, let not these things be a care to you in your mind.
sentences.i: “Take courage; do not let these things weigh on your mind.
sentences.n: Odysseus reassures his father. θάρσει is the imperative of θαρσέω ‘take courage’. μελόντων is the third plural present imperative of μέλω ‘be a care’, ‘let them not be a care’, with μή τοι ‘not … to you’. σῇσι is the possessive ‘your’ in the dative plural ending -ῃσι, agreeing with φρεσί ‘mind’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν προτὶ οἶκον, ὃς ὀρχάτου ἐγγύθι κεῖται·
sentences.l: But let us go to the house, which near the orchard lies;
sentences.i: But let us go to the house, which lies close to the orchard;
sentences.n: ἴομεν is a hortatory subjunctive, ‘let us go’ (Attic ἴωμεν). προτί is the epic form of πρός ‘to’. Here ὅς is the relative pronoun ‘which’, not the possessive. ὀρχάτου is the genitive of ὄρχατος ‘orchard’, and ἐγγύθι ‘near’ has the place-suffix -θι.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δὲ Τηλέμαχον καὶ βουκόλον ἠδὲ συβώτην
προὔπεμψ’, ὡς ἂν δεῖπνον ἐφοπλίσσωσι τάχιστα.
sentences.l:
and there Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
I sent ahead, so that the meal they may prepare most quickly.”
sentences.i: and I sent Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd ahead there, so that they may prepare the meal as quickly as possible.”
sentences.n: Odysseus tells his father who is waiting at the house; this unit ends his speech. προὔπεμψ’ is προὔπεμψα, the aorist of προπέμπω ‘send ahead’, with προ- and the augment fused. The cowherd is βουκόλος and the swineherd συβώτης, and neither is named here. ὡς ἂν ἐφοπλίσσωσι is purpose with the subjunctive, ‘so that they may make ready’; τάχιστα, the superlative adverb, is ‘as quickly as possible’.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσαντε βάτην πρὸς δώματα καλά.
sentences.l: So then having spoken, the two went to the fine halls.
sentences.i: So the two of them spoke, and went to the fine halls.
sentences.n: This unit begins a paragraph. φωνήσαντε and βάτην are both dual forms, nominative-dual participle and third-dual aorist of βαίνω, because exactly two people go, father and son; Attic would usually have plurals. The opening ὣς ἄρα φωνήσ- is the formula ‘so then having spoken’, here with the dual participle. καλά is ‘fine’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἵκοντο δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας,
εὗρον Τηλέμαχον καὶ βουκόλον ἠδὲ συβώτην
ταμνομένους κρέα πολλὰ κερῶντάς τ’ αἴθοπα οἶνον.
sentences.l:
And when then they reached the well-inhabited house,
they found Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd
cutting up much meat and mixing the fire-faced wine.
sentences.i: And when they reached the well-inhabited house, they found Telemachus and the cowherd and the swineherd cutting up much meat and mixing the wine that has the look of fire.
sentences.n: οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’, the two travellers, and ῥ’ is ῥα. ἵκοντο is an unaugmented aorist of ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive at’. δόμους εὖ ναιετάοντας ‘the well-inhabited house’ is a formula, with the plural for one house. εὗρον is ‘found’. ταμνομένους is the middle participle of τάμνω ‘cut (for themselves)’, and κερῶντας the participle of κεράω ‘mix’ (wine with water). αἴθοπα means ‘fire-faced’, from αἴθω ‘burn’ and ὄψ ‘face’, and it is translated every time.

sentences.t:
τόφρα δὲ Λαέρτην μεγαλήτορα ᾧ ἐνὶ οἴκῳ
ἀμφίπολος Σικελὴ λοῦσεν καὶ χρῖσεν ἐλαίῳ,
sentences.l:
And meanwhile Laertes, great-spirited, in his own house
a handmaid, a Sicel one, bathed and anointed with oil,
sentences.i: Meanwhile, in his own house, a Sicel handmaid bathed great-spirited Laertes and anointed him with oil,
sentences.n: The sentence runs across a paragraph break, so the unit is cut at the comma. τόφρα δέ is ‘and meanwhile’. ᾧ is the possessive ‘his own’, with ἐνί = ἐν. μεγαλήτορα, ‘great-spirited’, is Laertes’ epithet here and is translated every time. ἀμφίπολος is a ‘handmaid’, and Σικελή is ‘Sicel’, of the Sicels, a people of Sicily; a Sicel woman is named again at 389. λοῦσεν and χρῖσεν are the aorists of λούω ‘bathe’ and χρίω ‘anoint’; ἐλαίῳ is the dative of ἔλαιον ‘olive oil’.

sentences.t: ἀμφὶ δ’ ἄρα χλαῖναν καλὴν βάλεν·
sentences.l: and around him then a fine cloak she threw;
sentences.i: and she threw a fine cloak around him;
sentences.n: This unit begins Murray’s new paragraph, in the middle of the sentence begun in 365. ἀμφί … βάλεν is tmesis, ‘threw around’, with the augment dropped (Attic ἀμφέβαλεν). The subject is still the handmaid. χλαῖνα is a ‘cloak’ and καλήν ‘fine’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ἀθήνη
ἄγχι παρισταμένη μέλε’ ἤλδανε ποιμένι λαῶν,
μείζονα δ’ ἠὲ πάρος καὶ πάσσονα θῆκεν ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.l:
but Athena,
close by, standing near, made grow the limbs of the shepherd of the people,
taller than before and stouter she made him to look upon.
sentences.i: but Athena, standing close beside him, made the limbs of the shepherd of the people grow, and made him taller than before and stouter to look upon.
sentences.n: Athena transforms Laertes, and the ‘shepherd of the people’ is Laertes himself, a title for a king. παρισταμένη is ‘standing beside’. ἤλδανε is from ἀλδαίνω ‘make grow’, and μέλε’ is μέλεα ‘limbs’ with the vowel elided. μείζονα and πάσσονα are comparatives, ‘taller’ and ‘stouter’, agreeing with the unexpressed ‘him’; ἠέ is ‘than’ and πάρος ‘before’. θῆκεν ἰδέσθαι is ‘made him (to look)’, with an infinitive of respect.

sentences.t: ἐκ δ’ ἀσαμίνθου βῆ·
sentences.l: And out of the bath he stepped;
sentences.i: He stepped out of the bath;
sentences.n: Laertes is still the subject. ἀσάμινθος is a ‘bath’ in the sense of a tub; ἐκ … βῆ is ‘went out’, with the preverb ἐκ standing apart and βῆ without augment (Attic ἐξέβη). ‘He stepped out of the bath’ is the English of an earlier shipped bath-and-dress line.

sentences.t:
θαύμαζε δέ μιν φίλος υἱός,
ὡς ἴδεν ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιον ἄντην·
sentences.l:
and marvelled at him his dear son,
when he saw him like to the immortal gods to look upon;
sentences.i: and his dear son marvelled at him when he saw him, like the immortal gods to look upon;
sentences.n: Here φίλος υἱός, ‘dear son’, is Odysseus, who looks at his father. μιν is ‘him’, θαύμαζε the imperfect ‘marvelled’, and ὡς ἴδεν ‘when he saw’, with ἴδεν unaugmented. ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖς ἐναλίγκιον ἄντην is ‘like to the immortal gods to look upon’: ἐναλίγκιος means ‘like’, and ἄντην ‘face to face, to the eye’.

sentences.t: καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l: And, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: And lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: This is the speech-introduction formula for Odysseus. φωνήσας is ‘having raised his voice’, and προσηύδα the imperfect of προσαυδάω ‘speak to’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα, ‘winged words’, is translated the same way every time.

sentences.t:
ὦ πάτερ, ἦ μάλα τίς σε θεῶν αἰειγενετάων
εἶδός τε μέγεθός τε ἀμείνονα θῆκεν ἰδέσθαι.
sentences.l:
“O father, truly some one of the gods, the forever-born,
in form and in size better has made you to look upon.”
sentences.i: “Father, surely one of the everlasting gods has made you better to look upon, in form and in size.”
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks to his father in wonder. ὦ πάτερ is ‘father’. ἦ μάλα is ‘truly, surely’, and τίς … θεῶν is ‘some one of the gods’. αἰειγενετάων is a genitive plural in -άων (Attic -ῶν) of αἰειγενέτης ‘forever-born’, an epithet translated every time. εἶδός τε μέγεθός τε are accusatives of respect, ‘in form and in size’. ἀμείνονα is the comparative ‘better’, agreeing with σε, and θῆκεν ἰδέσθαι ‘made (you) better to look upon’ echoes 369.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖ Λαέρτης πεπνυμένος ἀντίον ηὔδα·
sentences.l: To him in turn prudent Laertes spoke, face to face:
sentences.i: Then prudent Laertes spoke to him in turn, face to face:
sentences.n: A reply-formula built from a name and an epithet: τὸν δ’ αὖ … ἀντίον ηὔδα. πεπνυμένος, ‘prudent’, is a standing epithet translated every time, and here it belongs to Laertes. ηὔδα is the imperfect of αὐδάω ‘speak’ (ἐ+αὐ → ηὐ), and ἀντίον ‘face to face’ is an adverb.

sentences.t:
αἲ γάρ, Ζεῦ τε πάτερ καὶ Ἀθηναίη καὶ Ἄπολλον,
οἷος Νήρικον εἷλον, ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον,
ἀκτὴν ἠπείροιο, Κεφαλλήνεσσιν ἀνάσσων,
sentences.l:
“Would that — Father Zeus, and Athena, and Apollo —
such as when Nericus I took, the well-built citadel,
a headland of the mainland, ruling over the Cephallenians,
sentences.i: “If only — Father Zeus, Athena, and Apollo — I were such a man as I was when I took Nericus, the well-built citadel, a headland of the mainland, ruling over the Cephallenians,
sentences.n: Laertes wishes himself young again, and the wish takes seven lines to finish; here it only begins. αἲ γάρ is ‘would that’, and the first line is the same as one shipped earlier. οἷος … εἷλον is ‘such as … I took’, the matching τοῖος coming at 379. Νήρικον is the town Nericus, and ἀκτὴν ἠπείροιο, ‘a headland of the mainland’, stands beside it. ἐϋκτίμενον πτολίεθρον is ‘well-built citadel’. ἀνάσσων ‘ruling’ takes the dative.

sentences.t:
τοῖος ἐών τοι χθιζὸς ἐν ἡμετέροισι δόμοισιν,
τεύχε’ ἔχων ὤμοισιν, ἐφεστάμεναι καὶ ἀμύνειν
ἄνδρας μνηστῆρας·
sentences.i: such a man, yesterday, in our house, with armour on my shoulders, to stand by you and ward off the suitors;
sentences.n: τοῖος ἐών ‘being such’ answers the οἷος of 377, and the wish goes on: to have stood beside Odysseus yesterday, armed. χθιζός, ‘of yesterday’, is an adjective used for an adverb. τεύχε’ is τεύχεα ‘armour’, and ὤμοισιν a dative plural ‘on my shoulders’. τοι is the enclitic dative ‘for you’. ἐφεστάμεναι is the infinitive of ἐφίστημι ‘stand by’, and ἀμύνειν ‘ward off’ takes the accusative of what is warded off. ἡμετέροισι ‘our’ shows the house belongs to both.

sentences.t:
τῷ κε σφέων γούνατ’ ἔλυσα
πολλῶν ἐν μεγάροισι, σὺ δὲ φρένας ἔνδον ἐγήθεις.
sentences.l:
then of them the knees I would have loosed
of many in the halls, and you in your mind within would have rejoiced.”
sentences.i: then I would have loosed the knees of many of them in the halls, and you would have been glad in your mind.”
sentences.n: Laertes finishes his wish. τῷ is ‘then, in that case’, and κε with the aorist ἔλυσα gives ‘I would have loosed’. σφέων is the Homeric genitive plural ‘of them’ (Attic αὐτῶν). γούνατ’ ἔλυσα, ‘I loosed the knees’, is the active of the idiom in 345 and means to strike down. κε is understood with ἐγήθεις, the imperfect of γηθέω ‘rejoice’, and φρένας ἔνδον is ‘in your mind within’.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν τοιαῦτα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἀγόρευον.
sentences.l: So they, such things to one another were saying;
sentences.i: So they talked in this way with one another;
sentences.n: A paragraph begins here, and the line is a scene-closing formula. οἱ μέν is ‘they, on the one hand’, picked up by the οἱ δέ of the next line. τοιαῦτα is ‘such things’, ἀλλήλους ‘one another’, and ἀγόρευον the imperfect of ἀγορεύω ‘speak’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν παύσαντο πόνου τετύκοντό τε δαῖτα,
ἑξείης ἕζοντο κατὰ κλισμούς τε θρόνους τε·
sentences.l:
And they, when then they had ceased from toil and had made ready the feast,
in order seated themselves along the seats and the chairs;
sentences.i: And when they had ended their labour and prepared the meal, they took their places in order along the seats and the chairs;
sentences.n: The meal is ready and the company sits. παύσαντο πόνου is ‘ceased from toil’, with a genitive of separation. τετύκοντο is a reduplicated aorist middle of τεύχω ‘make ready’. ἑξείης is ‘in order’. κλισμός and θρόνος are two kinds of seat, translated ‘seat’ and ‘chair’. Both lines are in the English of earlier shipped lines.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ οἱ μὲν δείπνῳ ἐπεχείρεον, ἀγχίμολον δὲ
ἦλθ’ ὁ γέρων Δολίος, σὺν δ’ υἱεῖς τοῖο γέροντος,
sentences.l:
There they, on the one hand, set their hands to the meal, and close by
came the old man Dolius, and with him the sons of that old man,
sentences.i: There they set their hands to the meal, and close by came old Dolius, and with him the sons of the old man,
sentences.n: Dolius and his sons now enter. οἱ μέν ‘they’ is answered by the δέ of ἀγχίμολον δέ, which opens the clause with ἦλθ’ ‘came’. ἐπεχείρεον is the uncontracted imperfect of ἐπιχειρέω ‘put one’s hand to’, with the dative δείπνῳ. ἀγχίμολον is an adverb, ‘close at hand’. ὁ γέρων Δολίος is ‘the old man Dolius’; σὺν δ’ is ‘and with’ him; υἱεῖς is ‘sons’; τοῖο is an old genitive of the pronoun, ‘of that’.

sentences.t:
ἐξ ἔργων μογέοντες, ἐπεὶ προμολοῦσα κάλεσσεν
μήτηρ γρηῦς Σικελή, ἥ σφεας τρέφε καί ῥα γέροντα
ἐνδυκέως κομέεσκεν, ἐπεὶ κατὰ γῆρας ἔμαρψεν.
sentences.l:
from their works toiling, since coming forward had called them
their mother, an old woman, a Sicel one, who them nurtured, and the old man
kindly used to tend, since old age had seized him.
sentences.i: toiling from their work, since their mother, an old Sicel woman, had come forward and called them, she who had reared them and kindly used to look after the old man, since old age had seized him.
sentences.n: Here is why the sons come late: they were working, and their mother called them in. ἐξ ἔργων is ‘from their work’, and μογέοντες ‘toiling’. προμολοῦσα is the aorist participle of προβλώσκω ‘come forward’. γρηῦς is ‘old woman’; a Sicel woman has been named at 366 too, and the text does not say whether she is the same; ἥ σφεας is ‘she who … them’, with σφεας the Ionic accusative of the pronoun. κομέεσκεν is an iterative imperfect in -εσκ-, ‘used to tend’. κατά … ἔμαρψεν is tmesis, ‘seized’. The words ‘kindly used to tend the old man’ are those of an earlier shipped line.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ὡς οὖν Ὀδυσῆα ἴδον φράσσαντό τε θυμῷ,
ἔσταν ἐνὶ μεγάροισι τεθηπότες·
sentences.l:
And they, when then Odysseus they saw and noticed in their mind,
stood in the halls, amazed;
sentences.i: And when they saw Odysseus and took note of him in their minds, they stood in the halls, amazed;
sentences.n: The newcomers react to the sight of Odysseus. οἱ δ’ is ‘and they’, and ὡς οὖν ‘when then’. ἴδον is an unaugmented aorist, and φράσσαντο is the aorist middle of φράζομαι ‘take note of’, with θυμῷ ‘in their mind’. ἔσταν is ἔστησαν, the intransitive aorist ‘they stood’. τεθηπότες is the perfect participle of a verb meaning ‘be astonished’, ‘amazed’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ Ὀδυσσεὺς
μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι καθαπτόμενος προσέειπεν·
sentences.l:
but Odysseus,
with gentle words accosting, addressed them:
sentences.i: but Odysseus spoke to them, addressing them directly with gentle words:
sentences.n: αὐτάρ ‘but’ turns to Odysseus. μειλιχίοις ἐπέεσσι is a dative of means, ‘with gentle words’; μειλίχιος is ‘gentle, soft’. καθαπτόμενος προσέειπεν, ‘accosting, he addressed’, is rendered ‘addressing them directly’ because the verb does not by itself carry reproach.

sentences.t: ὦ γέρον, ἵζ’ ἐπὶ δεῖπνον, ἀπεκλελάθεσθε δὲ θάμβευς·
sentences.l: “O old man, sit to the meal, and forget your amazement;
sentences.i: “Old man, sit down to the meal, and forget your amazement;
sentences.n: Odysseus speaks first to Dolius. ὦ γέρον is ‘old man’. ἵζ’ is ἵζε, the imperative of ἵζω ‘sit’. ἀπεκλελάθεσθε is a plural imperative, though the address is to one man: Odysseus speaks to Dolius and through him to his sons. It means ‘forget’, and θάμβευς is the Ionic genitive of θάμβος ‘amazement’ (Attic θάμβους), the genitive that goes with a verb of forgetting.

sentences.t:
δηρὸν γὰρ σίτῳ ἐπιχειρήσειν μεμαῶτες
μίμνομεν ἐν μεγάροις, ὑμέας ποτιδέγμενοι αἰεί.
sentences.l:
for long to the food to set our hands eager
we have waited in the halls, you awaiting always.”
sentences.i: For we have long been waiting in the halls, eager to set our hands to the food, always looking out for you.”
sentences.n: δηρόν is ‘for a long time’. μεμαῶτες is the perfect participle ‘eager’, with the future infinitive ἐπιχειρήσειν ‘to set the hand to’ and the dative σίτῳ ‘food’. μίμνομεν is a present with the force of ‘we have been waiting’. ὑμέας is the Ionic accusative of ‘you’ (Attic ὑμᾶς), and ποτιδέγμενοι, an epic participle of δέχομαι with ποτί = πρός, means ‘waiting for’. αἰεί is ‘always’.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρ ἔφη, Δολίος δ’ ἰθὺς κίε χεῖρε πετάσσας
ἀμφοτέρας, Ὀδυσεῦς δὲ λαβὼν κύσε χεῖρ’ ἐπὶ καρπῷ,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
So then he spoke, and Dolius straight went, stretching out
both hands, and of Odysseus, taking it, he kissed the hand on the wrist,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Dolius went straight up to him with both hands stretched out, and took Odysseus’ hand and kissed it at the wrist, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: A paragraph begins, and Dolius greets Odysseus. ὣς ἄρ ἔφη is ‘so he spoke’ (the edition prints no mark after ἄρ). κίε is the unaugmented ‘went’, ἰθύς ‘straight’, and πετάσσας ‘having spread out’. χεῖρε is a dual, ‘the two hands’, and ἀμφοτέρας ‘both’ follows in the plural form. Ὀδυσεῦς is a genitive, the short form beside Ὀδυσῆος. κύσε is ‘kissed’, and καρπῷ ‘wrist’. The last line is the winged-words formula.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλ’, ἐπεὶ νόστησας ἐελδομένοισι μάλ’ ἡμῖν
οὐδ’ ἔτ’ ὀϊομένοισι, θεοὶ δέ σ’ ἀνήγαγον αὐτοί,
οὖλέ τε καὶ μάλα χαῖρε, θεοὶ δέ τοι ὄλβια δοῖεν.
sentences.l:
“O friend, since you came home to us, longing very much
and no longer expecting, and the gods led you back themselves,
be well and welcome greatly, and to you the gods blessings may give.
sentences.i: “Friend, since you have come home to us, who longed for it so much and no longer expected it, and the gods themselves have brought you back, be well and heartily welcome, and may the gods give you blessings.
sentences.n: Dolius’s greeting is long, and the sentence is built round a ‘since’ clause. νόστησας is the aorist of νοστέω ‘come home’; ἐελδομένοισι (from ἔλδομαι ‘long for’) and ὀϊομένοισι (ὀΐομαι ‘expect’) are datives agreeing with ἡμῖν ‘to us’. θεοὶ … ἀνήγαγον αὐτοί is ‘the gods themselves led you back’. οὖλε is a wish for health, ‘be well’; its exact form is unclear. χαῖρε is ‘welcome’. ὄλβια is ‘blessings, prosperity’, and δοῖεν the optative ‘may they give’.

sentences.t:
καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον, ὄφρ’ ἐῢ εἰδῶ,
ἢ ἤδη σάφα οἶδε περίφρων Πηνελόπεια
νοστήσαντά σε δεῦρ’, ἦ ἄγγελον ὀτρύνωμεν.
sentences.l:
And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well,
whether already clearly knows circumspect Penelope
that you have come home here, or a messenger we should send.”
sentences.i: And tell me this truly, so that I may know it well, whether circumspect Penelope already knows for certain that you have come home, or whether we should send a messenger.”
sentences.n: Dolius asks whether Penelope has been told. καί μοι τοῦτ’ ἀγόρευσον ἐτήτυμον ‘tell me this truly’ is as shipped earlier; ὄφρα with the subjunctive εἰδῶ gives ‘so that I may know’. ἢ … ἦ is ‘whether … or’, and σάφα ‘clearly, for certain’. περίφρων Πηνελόπεια, ‘circumspect Penelope’, carries its epithet every time. νοστήσαντά σε is accusative plus participle, ‘that you have come home’, and ὀτρύνωμεν is a deliberative subjunctive, ‘should we send’.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πολύμητις Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed many-wiled Odysseus:
sentences.i: In answer Odysseus of many wiles said to him:
sentences.n: The reply-formula of 330 and 356 once more, with the same English. Odysseus is the speaker, and what he says in answer is only two short sentences.

sentences.t: ὦ γέρον, ἤδη οἶδε·
sentences.l: “O old man, already she knows;
sentences.i: “Old man, she knows already;
sentences.n: Odysseus calls Dolius ‘old man’ again. ἤδη is ‘already’, and οἶδε the perfect with present sense, ‘she knows’, the verb of 404 (σάφα οἶδε) given back. The short sentence answers the question.

sentences.t: τί σε χρὴ ταῦτα πένεσθαι;
sentences.l: why need you these things busy yourself about?”
sentences.i: why should you busy yourself about this?”
sentences.n: τί is ‘why’, and σε χρή ‘it is necessary for you’, so ‘why must you’. πένεσθαι is the infinitive of πένομαι ‘busy oneself, toil at’, not ‘be poor’; the same verb returns at 412. Odysseus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δ’ αὖτις ἄρ’ ἕζετ’ ἐϋξέστου ἐπὶ δίφρου.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and he again then sat on the well-polished stool.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and Dolius sat down again on the well-polished stool.
sentences.n: This unit begins a paragraph and shows Dolius sitting down as he has been told. φάθ’ is φάτο, the aorist of φημί, with its last vowel elided and τ turned to θ before the rough breathing of ὁ. ὁ δ’ is ‘and he’, Dolius. αὖτις is ‘again’, ἕζετ’ = ἕζετο ‘seated himself’, ἐϋξέστου ‘well-polished’, and δίφρου the genitive of δίφρος ‘stool’.

sentences.t:
ὣς δ’ αὔτως παῖδες Δολίου κλυτὸν ἀμφ’ Ὀδυσῆα
δεικανόωντ’ ἐπέεσσι καὶ ἐν χείρεσσι φύοντο,
ἑξείης δ’ ἕζοντο παραὶ Δολίον, πατέρα σφόν.
sentences.l:
And in the same way the sons of Dolius around famous Odysseus
welcomed him with words and on his hands clung,
in order sat beside Dolius, their father.
sentences.i: In the same way the sons of Dolius crowded round famous Odysseus, welcoming him with words and clinging to his hands, and took their places in order beside Dolius, their father.
sentences.n: The sons follow their father’s example. ὣς δ’ αὔτως is ‘and in just the same way’; κλυτόν is ‘famous’, a stock epithet translated every time. δεικανόωντ’ is the imperfect of δεικανάομαι ‘greet, welcome’ (the root is uncertain), uncontracted and elided. φύοντο is the imperfect of φύω in the middle voice, which usually means ‘grow’, so ἐν χείρεσσι φύοντο is ‘clung to his hands’. σφόν is the possessive ‘their’, from σφός.

sentences.t: ὣς οἱ μὲν περὶ δεῖπνον ἐνὶ μεγάροισι πένοντο·
sentences.l: So they were busied about the meal in the halls.
sentences.i: So they busied themselves with the meal in the halls.
sentences.n: This unit begins a paragraph and closes the scene in the house; its English is the shipped English of the same line. οἱ μέν is ‘they, on the one hand’, answered by the δέ in 413 where Rumour is introduced. πένοντο is the imperfect of πένομαι ‘busy oneself’, the verb of 407, and περὶ δεῖπνον is ‘about the meal’.

sentences.t:
Ὄσσα δ’ ἄρ’ ἄγγελος ὦκα κατὰ πτόλιν ᾤχετο πάντη,
μνηστήρων στυγερὸν θάνατον καὶ κῆρ’ ἐνέπουσα.
sentences.l:
And Rumour, a messenger, swiftly through the city went everywhere,
the suitors’ hateful death and doom proclaiming.
sentences.i: Meanwhile Rumour, the messenger, went swiftly everywhere through the city, telling of the suitors’ hateful death and doom.
sentences.n: Ὄσσα, ‘Rumour’, is a word for a voice or report; the edition capitalises it, treating it as a person who goes through the city as a messenger. πτόλιν is the old form of πόλιν. ᾤχετο is the imperfect of οἴχομαι ‘go’, and πάντῃ ‘everywhere’. κῆρ’ is κῆρα, the accusative of the feminine κήρ ‘doom, fate of death’, and not the neuter κῆρ ‘heart’ that follows at 420. ἐνέπουσα is ‘telling of, proclaiming’.

sentences.t:
οἱ δ’ ἄρ’ ὁμῶς ἀΐοντες ἐφοίτων ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος
μυχμῷ τε στοναχῇ τε δόμων προπάροιθ’ Ὀδυσῆος,
sentences.l:
And they, then, alike hearing came, one from one place and another,
with moan and with groan before the house of Odysseus,
sentences.i: And all who heard it came, one from one place and one from another, with moaning and groaning, to the front of the house of Odysseus,
sentences.n: The townspeople come to the house. ἀΐοντες is the uncontracted ‘hearing’, and ὁμῶς ‘alike, all together’. ἐφοίτων is the imperfect ‘kept coming’. ἄλλοθεν ἄλλος, ‘one from one place, another from another’, uses the suffix -θεν ‘from’. μυχμῷ and στοναχῇ are datives of manner: μυχμός is a ‘moaning’, from a verb for a low cry, and στοναχή a ‘groaning’. προπάροιθ’ is προπάροιθε ‘in front of’ with the genitive, and δόμων is a plural for one house.

sentences.t:
ἐκ δὲ νέκυς οἴκων φόρεον καὶ θάπτον ἕκαστοι,
τοὺς δ’ ἐξ ἀλλάων πολίων οἶκόνδε ἕκαστον
πέμπον ἄγειν ἁλιεῦσι θοῇς ἐπὶ νηυσὶ τιθέντες·
sentences.i: They carried the dead out of the house and buried them, each group its own, and those from other cities they sent home, each one to his own place, putting them on swift ships in the care of fishermen;
sentences.n: The dead suitors are removed. ἐκ … φόρεον is tmesis, ‘carried out’; νέκυς is the accusative plural of νέκυς ‘corpse’, and οἴκων, a plural for the one house, is ‘from the house’; θάπτον is ‘were burying’; ἕκαστοι ‘each group’ (the men of each family). τοὺς δ’ introduces the dead from outside, with ἀλλάων, the Homeric genitive plural of ἄλλος. οἶκόνδε ‘homeward’ has the suffix -δε. ἄγειν is an infinitive of purpose, ‘to convey’. ἁλιεῦσι is a dative, ‘to fishermen’, and the construction is loose: the dead are put aboard ships and handed to the fishermen who sail them.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ δ’ εἰς ἀγορὴν κίον ἀθρόοι, ἀχνύμενοι κῆρ.
sentences.l: And they themselves to the assembly went, all together, grieving in heart.
sentences.i: They themselves went to the assembly in a body, grieving in heart.
sentences.n: αὐτοί ‘they themselves’ turns from the dead to the living men of Ithaca. ἀγορή is the ‘assembly’, and κίον the unaugmented ‘went’. ἀθρόοι is ‘in a body, all together’. κῆρ here is the neuter ‘heart’, an accusative of respect, ‘grieving in heart’, and not the κήρ ‘doom’ of 414. The English of the first half is that of a line shipped earlier.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ἤγερθεν ὁμηγερέες τ’ ἐγένοντο,
τοῖσιν δ’ Εὐπείθης ἀνά θ’ ἵστατο καὶ μετέειπε·
sentences.l:
But when they were gathered and assembled-together had become,
and before them Eupeithes up stood and spoke among them:
sentences.i: When they had gathered and were all assembled, Eupeithes stood up among them and spoke:
sentences.n: Eupeithes is the father of Antinous, as the next two lines say. ἤγερθεν is the aorist passive of ἀγείρω ‘were gathered’, and ὁμηγερέες ‘assembled together’. τοῖσιν is a dative, ‘before them’. ἀνά … ἵστατο is tmesis, ‘stood up’, with θ’ for τε, and μετέειπε means ‘spoke among’. The first line is in the English of an earlier line.

sentences.t:
παιδὸς γάρ οἱ ἄλαστον ἐνὶ φρεσὶ πένθος ἔκειτο,
Ἀντινόου, τὸν πρῶτον ἐνήρατο δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.l:
For of his son unforgettable grief in his mind lay,
of Antinous, whom first had slain heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: For the grief for his son lay in his mind, a grief he could not forget — for Antinous, whom heavenly Odysseus had killed first:
sentences.n: These lines say why Eupeithes speaks. παιδός and Ἀντινόου are genitives of the person grieved for, with οἱ ‘his’ and ἔκειτο ‘lay’. ἄλαστον is traditionally ‘not to be forgotten’, though some ancient readers took it as ‘unbearable’, and its root is uncertain. ἐνήρατο is the aorist middle of ἐναίρω ‘slay’, and τὸν πρῶτον is ‘the first’. The epithet δῖος, ‘heavenly’, is kept even here, because it belongs to the poet’s phrase, not to Eupeithes’ feelings.

sentences.t: τοῦ ὅ γε δάκρυ χέων ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν·
sentences.l: For him he, a tear shedding, addressed-the-assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.i: Shedding tears for him, he addressed the assembly and spoke among them:
sentences.n: τοῦ is the pronoun in the genitive, ‘for him’, that is, for his son. ὅ γε is ‘he’. δάκρυ χέων is ‘shedding tears’, with the singular δάκρυ standing for tears in general. ἀγορήσατο καὶ μετέειπεν is a pair of verbs, ‘addressed the assembly’ and ‘spoke among them’.

sentences.t: ὦ φίλοι, ἦ μέγα ἔργον ἀνὴρ ὅδ’ ἐμήσατ’ Ἀχαιούς·
sentences.l: “O friends, truly a great deed this man has devised against the Achaeans:
sentences.i: “Friends, this man has devised a truly great deed against the Achaeans:
sentences.n: Eupeithes’ speech begins a paragraph; he never names Odysseus, only ἀνὴρ ὅδε ‘this man’. ὦ φίλοι is ‘friends’. ἦ μέγα ἔργον is ‘truly a great deed’. ἐμήσατ’ is ἐμήσατο, the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise, plan’. Ἀχαιούς is an accusative of the people affected, ‘against the Achaeans’, and ‘Achaeans’ here means the Greeks of the islands in general, among whom Eupeithes counts the Cephallenians of 429.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν σὺν νήεσσιν ἄγων πολέας τε καὶ ἐσθλοὺς
ὤλεσε μὲν νῆας γλαφυράς, ἀπὸ δ’ ὤλεσε λαούς·
sentences.l:
Those, on the one hand, with ships leading, many and good,
he lost the hollow ships, and lost the men;
sentences.i: Some of them he led away in ships, many and good men, and he lost the hollow ships and lost the men;
sentences.n: τοὺς μέν is answered by τοὺς δέ in the next unit, ‘some … others’. νήεσσιν is the Ionic dative plural of νηῦς ‘ship’, and ἄγων ‘leading’. πολέας is ‘many’ and ἐσθλούς ‘good’. ὤλεσε is the aorist of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy, lose’, and ἀπὸ … ὤλεσε is tmesis. γλαφυράς is ‘hollow’, and λαούς the accusative of λαός ‘people, men’. The complaint here is the loss of the first body of men.

sentences.t:
τοὺς δ’ ἐλθὼν ἔκτεινε Κεφαλλήνων ὄχ’ ἀρίστους,
ἀλλ’ ἄγετε, πρὶν τοῦτον ἢ ἐς Πύλον ὦκα ἱκέσθαι
ἢ καὶ ἐς Ἤλιδα δῖαν, ὅθι κρατέουσιν Ἐπειοί,
ἴομεν·
sentences.l:
and these, going, he killed, by far the best of the Cephallenians,
but come, before this man either to Pylos swiftly arrives
or even to heavenly Elis, where the Epeans hold sway,
let us go;
sentences.i: and the others he came and killed, by far the best of the Cephallenians. But come, let us go before this man reaches Pylos in haste, or even heavenly Elis, where the Epeans hold sway;
sentences.n: τοὺς δέ ‘and those’ answers τοὺς μέν. ἐλθών is ‘having come’, and ὄχ’ is ὄχα ‘by far’, with the superlative ἀρίστους. Κεφαλλήνων is ‘of the Cephallenians’. πρίν takes the infinitive ἱκέσθαι ‘reach’, with τοῦτον as its subject; ἢ … ἢ καί is ‘either … or even’. Ἤλιδα δῖαν ‘heavenly Elis’ and ὅθι κρατέουσιν Ἐπειοί ‘where the Epeans hold sway’ are in the English of an earlier line. ἴομεν is the hortatory subjunctive; the sentence ends after it at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: ἦ καὶ ἔπειτα κατηφέες ἐσσόμεθ’ αἰεί·
sentences.l: truly even afterwards downcast we shall be always:
sentences.i: Truly, afterwards too we shall be downcast for ever;
sentences.n: ἦ καὶ ἔπειτα is ‘truly even afterwards’. κατηφέες, nominative plural of κατηφής, is ‘downcast, dejected’ (the word looks like ‘with eyes cast down’). ἐσσόμεθ’ is ἐσσόμεθα, the future of εἰμί with the doubled σ of epic, and αἰεί is ‘always’. The next sentence gives the reason, introduced by γάρ.

sentences.t:
λώβη γὰρ τάδε γ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ἐσσομένοισι πυθέσθαι,
εἰ δὴ μὴ παίδων τε κασιγνήτων τε φονῆας
τισόμεθ’.
sentences.l:
For an outrage these things at least are, even for those to come, to hear of,
if indeed we shall not the killers of sons and of brothers
take vengeance on.
sentences.i: For this is an outrage, even for those yet to come to hear of, if we do not take vengeance on the killers of our sons and brothers.
sentences.n: λώβη is the plain noun ‘outrage’, a word of shameful treatment. τάδε γ’ is ‘these things at least’. ἐσσομένοισι is a dative plural participle of εἰμί, ‘for those who will be’, and πυθέσθαι ‘to learn’ is an infinitive saying what the outrage is for them. εἰ δὴ μή is ‘if indeed not’. παίδων τε κασιγνήτων τε is ‘of sons and of brothers’. τισόμεθ’ is the future of τίνυμαι ‘take vengeance on’, with φονῆας ‘killers’ as its object.

sentences.t:
οὐκ ἂν ἐμοί γε μετὰ φρεσὶν ἡδὺ γένοιτο
ζωέμεν, ἀλλὰ τάχιστα θανὼν φθιμένοισι μετείην.
sentences.l:
Not would to me, at least, in my mind sweet become
to live, but most quickly having died among the dead may I be.
sentences.i: For my part, life would not be sweet to me in my mind; no, let me die as quickly as I can and be among the dead.
sentences.n: Eupeithes states his own resolve. οὐκ ἂν … γένοιτο is a potential optative, ‘would not become’; ἡδύ is ‘sweet’. ζωέμεν is the infinitive of ζώω ‘live’ in -έμεν (Attic ζῆν). In ἀλλὰ τάχιστα θανών the participle θανών ‘having died’ is joined to the wish-optative μετείην, from μέτειμι ‘be among’; φθιμένοισι is a dative plural ‘the dead’, from φθίνω ‘perish’. τάχιστα is ‘as quickly as possible’.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν, μὴ φθέωσι περαιωθέντες ἐκεῖνοι.
sentences.l: But let us go, lest they be beforehand, having crossed over, those men.”
sentences.i: But let us go, or else those men may cross over and get ahead of us.”
sentences.n: ἴομεν is again the hortatory subjunctive. μὴ φθέωσι is a fear-clause, ‘lest they be first’, with the uncontracted subjunctive of φθάνω ‘anticipate, be beforehand’. περαιωθέντες is the aorist passive participle of περαιόομαι ‘cross over’ (presumably the sea, on the way to Pylos or Elis), and ἐκεῖνοι ‘those men’ means Odysseus and his party. This is the last line of Eupeithes’ speech and of the part.
